_doc: The Human Baseline - Linear Narrative Dialogue Nodes Graph (No branching, pure storytelling).

nodes.text: Late Friday afternoon at Pete's Auto Care. The shop is filled with the steady rhythm of three active bays: the hiss of pneumatic lines, the low thrum of the air compressor, and classic rock drifting from a grease-spotted radio on the workbench.
Hand me that three-eighths torque wrench, Pete. Setting tension on this timing belt tensioner pulley. Forty-two foot-pounds, exactly where she wants to sit.

Pete slides the calibrated wrench across the rolling cart. Across the bay, three customer invoices sit neatly in the pickup rack, each marked 'PAID - PICKUP BY 5:30.' In Year Zero, when an engine rolls into the bay, people have the money to fix it.
Click. Perfect. She's lined up TDC. Another hundred thousand miles on this engine if they don't neglect their coolant flushes.

Phone buzzes on the tool chest. Text from Adriana: 'Truck arrived on time. Five pallets cleared, displays built, all four clerks showed up with energy. We're locking the registers at 7. Don't burn the burgers tonight.'

Todd wipes his hands on a clean red shop rag, rolls down the bay door, and clocks out on the analog punch clock. Outside, the early autumn breeze is clean. Across town at Oakridge Liquors, Adriana is wrapping up her shift.

Inside the bright, orderly aisles of Oakridge Liquors, the shelves are neatly fronted and faced. Warm amber bottles of Kentucky bourbon gleam under recessed halogen lights. Two young college students, Sam and Chloe, are chatting cheerfully behind register one.
Great job clearing the delivery skids today, you two. Take your full thirty-minute lunch breaks—no rushing. The weekend promotional endcap looks sharp.

There are no automated cameras counting Chloe's keystrokes. No algorithm shaving twelve minutes from Sam's timecard to appease an executive dashboard. Labor hours are managed with human trust, common sense, and mutual respect.
Drawer count balances down to the penny. Alarm set, doors locked. Time to head home for the cookout.

Twilight settles over Todd and Adriana's suburban patio. The charcoal kettle grill fills the backyard with the aroma of caramelized beef, toasted brioche buns, and charred peppers. Ice clinks in a cooler beside the deck table.

Guys, I'm telling you, our senior vice president dropped by our standup today. He said if we hit our Q4 deliverables, the entire junior engineering cohort is getting bumped up to full mid-level salaries. Full health benefits, four percent 401(k) match, the works!
That's huge, Marcus. You busted your tail on that degree, and it's paying off. Drink to that.
Just don't start buying imported scotch until the contract is signed in ink, Marcus. I see guys in my store celebrate early all the time.

Haha, deal! Though our lead architect did mention they're testing out some new automated syntax assistants next month. Says it's going to make us so productive we might never have to work overtime again.
Careful with tools that promise to do the thinking for you. In the shop, an automated diagnostic scanner is only as smart as the technician holding the test probe.

Laughter ripples around the patio table as the stars begin to emerge over quiet rooftops. Glasses clink. The future feels linear, stable, and welcoming—unaware of the silent algorithmic tremors already preparing to ripple beneath the economy.
End of Act I: The Warm Engine. This was the baseline: a world of steady hours, predictable ladders, and honest wages.

Eighteen months later. Inside the Oakridge Liquors breakroom, the paper schedule on the corkboard has been replaced by a sleek, wall-mounted corporate tablet. A small blinking digital indicator reads: 'WFM OPTIMIZATION ACTIVE - REVISION 4.12.'
Chloe, let me look at your phone. Did your schedule ping change again?

Chloe, a college junior balancing tuition payments, holds up her cracked screen with a strained look. Her Tuesday shift—historically a clean four hours from 2:00 to 6:00 PM—has been shaved down to 2:00 to 5:48 PM. Twelve minutes trimmed.

Twelve minutes. Corporate says the dynamic foot-traffic algorithm predicts an 8% drop in customer density between 5:45 and 6:00. Across forty regional stores, that trims eighty thousand dollars in operating payroll a quarter.

Nobody gets fired. No WARN notices are triggered. But Chloe's paycheck is thirty dollars lighter this week, and the grocery distributor's delivery truck doesn't care about dynamic foot traffic—the pallets still arrive at 5:30.
Don't sweat the twelve minutes today, Chloe. Clock out when the tablet says so. I'll haul the last two pallets of vodka into the cooler myself.

Tuesday, 11:30 AM at Pete's Auto Care. Todd is under the hood of a dark grey hatchback, checking the oil cap and running a fluid inspection. The bell rings as Marcus steps out of the customer waiting room into the bay.
Filter's replaced, Marcus. Synthetic 0W-20 topped off. Tires look good for another ten thousand miles. You're set.

Thanks, Todd. Man, it's nice to step away from the screen for an hour. Our new automated engineering scaffolding went live last month, and it is insane. It generates our database schemas and write-ups in seconds.
Sounds like smooth sailing then. You guys still expanding the team?

That's the weird part. Our junior recruiter was reassigned last week. We had three open junior software requisitions listed on our portal, and they all just disappeared. Leadership said our current team can handle double the velocity now without backfilling.
If two mechanics with a hydraulic lift can suddenly change eight sets of tires an hour, Pete doesn't hire a third guy. He pocketed the efficiency. Just keep your eye on the ladder, Marcus.

Tuesday night, 8:45 PM. Two steaming mugs of chamomile tea sit on the laminate kitchen table between Todd and Adriana. The local news murmurs quietly from the television in the background, reporting on tech sector hiring pauses and suburban retail performance.

My shoulders are burning. Corporate trimmed thirty-six total clerk hours off our weekly department budget. My clerks are stressed about making rent, and I'm the one who has to explain why the machine took their shift time.
Marcus came by for an oil change today. His company froze junior hiring. Said the automated software writes their boilerplate code now.

Look at this grocery receipt from yesterday, Todd. Eggs, chicken breast, coffee—up another 12%. If people's hours are getting shaved and junior salaries aren't getting paid, who is going to keep buying the groceries?
People still need their cars to run, and they still need your shelves stocked. Our hands do real work, Ade. We just have to stay tight on the margins and watch each other's backs.

Adriana leans back and smiles faintly, her hand resting over Todd's calloused fingers. The household is solvent and their work ethic is unshakeable. But outside in the suburban dark, the quiet tremors of the economic realignment have begun.
End of Act II: The First Tremors. The efficiency algorithms have taken root. Ahead lies Act III: The Severed Ladder.

Two years later. Sunday afternoon on the back patio. Marcus sits in a fold-out lawn chair, staring down at a blank laptop screen with dark circles under his eyes. A stack of printed resume drafts rests weighted down by an empty mug.
Drink some water, Marcus. You've been staring at that portal for three hours straight.

Four hundred and eighteen, Todd. That's the count. Four hundred and eighteen applications submitted over five months. Junior developer, QA tester, IT support, technical documentation—everything. Two screening calls, and then an automated rejection email forty-eight hours later.

Marcus wasn't laid off because he failed. His firm had thirty engineers; with generative software scaffolding, eight senior architects now do the output of thirty. The junior tier wasn't trimmed—it was systematically erased.
The student loans don't pause while the algorithms optimize, do they?

Seven hundred and forty dollars a month. Every single month. My emergency fund runs out in thirty days. If I don't land something that pays hourly by the first of next month, I have to give up my apartment and move into my parents' basement.
Monday morning inside Adriana's tiny back office at Oakridge Liquors. The metal desk is overflowing with paper job applications. A corporate hiring directive sits on her clipboard.
Look at this stack. One part-time stocking position. Sixteen hours a week at fifteen dollars an hour. Forty-two applications in forty-eight hours.

Adriana flips through the pages. Two years ago, these applications came from local community college kids looking for spending cash. Today, she's holding resumes from a 29-year-old former commercial copywriter, a 34-year-old corporate paralegal, and a junior accountant whose firm automated audit reviews.

They all say the same thing in the cover letter: 'Fast learner, reliable, physically capable, willing to take any shifts.' People with master's degrees asking if they can please unload Miller Lite cases on Saturday nights.
The desk-job economy has begun spilling directly into physical retail, not out of passion, but out of sheer survival desperation to service debt and buy groceries.

Tuesday afternoon at Pete's Auto Care. Marcus's compact hatchback sits in Bay 3 with its hood propped. The engine idles with a rough, shuddering shake, and the instrument cluster glows with an urgent amber 'SERVICE REQUIRED' alert.

I took it by the dealership on my way here, Todd. The service advisor told me they couldn't even tell me what the code meant without charging a three-hundred-and-eighty-dollar diagnostic cloud gateway access fee. I don't have three hundred and eighty dollars.

That's their new trick. They locked the CAN-bus architecture behind an encrypted telematics gateway. They want independent garages locked out so customers are forced to pay corporate subscription rates to clear a sensor fault.
Todd reaches into his rolling tool cart and pulls out a custom OBD-II breakout harness he soldered himself, paired with an open-source oscilloscope tablet running community right-to-repair firmware.
Pins 6 and 14 probed directly. Bypassing their cloud paywall. There she is: Bank 1 upstream O2 sensor heater circuit open. It's not a dead engine, Marcus. It's a sixty-dollar Bosch sensor.
Man... Todd, thank you. Seriously. Without this car, I can't even drive to do gig deliveries if things fall through.
Pay me for the part whenever you land your next gig, Marcus. We're keeping this car on the road. The machines only lock us out if we let them.
Todd ratchets the new oxygen sensor into the exhaust manifold with a clean, satisfying turn of his wrench. The check engine light goes dark. The engine purrs with steady, honest compression.
End of Act III: The Severed Ladder. The junior corporate rungs have shattered. Next lies Act IV: The Commuter Drain.

Year Five. Wednesday, 10:00 AM at Pete's Auto Care. The shop is unnervingly quiet. Bay 2 and Bay 3 stand empty, their concrete floors freshly mopped and dry. The daily roar of highway traffic along the commercial bypass has subdued into a sparse hum.
Only three cars on the board today, Pete. Two oil changes and a tire patch. We used to have eight vehicles stacked up outside by nine in the morning.

Pete leans against the service counter, reviewing the monthly car counts. When the office towers downtown emptied and middle-management jobs were absorbed by cloud software, suburban Vehicle Miles Traveled collapsed by 26%. Cars sit idle in driveways. Oil change intervals stretch from four months to fourteen.
People aren't driving forty miles a day into the city anymore. And when they do need work, they're driving on bald tires and ignoring brake squeals because groceries and rent eat everything.

A screeching grinding sound echoes off the pavement outside as an older compact crossover pulls into Bay 1. Elena, a 38-year-old mother working sixteen-hour days between two package delivery apps, steps out wincing.
Elena, step back for a second. Let me pull the front driver wheel. I heard that rotor from two blocks away.
Todd pulls the caliper. The friction material is completely gone; the steel brake backing plate has gouged deep, jagged trenches into the cast iron rotor. Metal shavings glisten on the shop floor.
Elena, the dealership or a franchise chain would quote you seven hundred dollars to replace all four corners with dealer OEM parts.

Elena's voice shakes: 'Todd, please. If this car doesn't pass inspection by Friday, the delivery app deactivates my account. I have eighty-five dollars in checking until my direct deposit hits Sunday night.'

Listen to me. I've got two resurfaced commercial rotors on the back shelf that fit this hub, and a clean set of ceramic pads Pete wholesale-ordered last week. You pay me fifty bucks for the pads today. I'm waiving the labor. You keep driving, and you keep feeding your kids.

Elena wipes her eyes as Todd's impact wrench zips the lug nuts back on. The trade is surviving not on corporate volume, but on community trust and mutual preservation. Across town, Adriana is battling the corporate retail response.

Friday, 5:30 PM at Oakridge Liquors. The four traditional cashier lanes have been ripped out, replaced by six automated self-checkout kiosks under blinding overhead cameras. Four of the six kiosks are frozen with blinking red overhead lights: 'ATTENDANT ASSISTANCE REQUIRED.'
Key override on kiosk three. Scanning ID on kiosk five. Folks, I apologize for the wait, I am the only floor manager authorized to clear age-verification lockouts right now.

Corporate promised the self-checkout grid would save 25% on store labor. Instead, it created chaos. Desperation-driven shoplifting skyrocketed; bottles of mid-tier tequila and whiskey walked out unnoticed during peak rush hours.

Corporate's solution wasn't to hire cashiers back. Their solution was to order sixty plexiglass lock-boxes. Now even twenty-dollar vodka is locked behind keyed glass. Every single customer has to ring a buzzer and wait for me to unlock a five-dollar item.

Shoppers grumble and abandon carts in the aisles. The friction of unstaffed automation has made shopping a frustrating ordeal, yet corporate district managers issue memos blaming store staff for declining customer satisfaction scores.
They want the profit of a machine, but the accountability of a human. As long as I'm holding these keys, they're not breaking my floor crew.
End of Act IV: The Commuter Drain. Mechanical volume has dropped and storefront friction has tightened. Ahead lies Act V: The Middle-Age Squeeze.
